note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 60; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 8) on data/benches/yield.json: copper hydroxide precipitated from weighed copper sulfate by an excess of sodium hydroxide, filtered and weighed; its percent yield.
title: Experiment: limiting reagent and percent yield

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: You will make copper hydroxide from copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide, and weigh what you get. What percent of the amount the equation says do you expect to recover? Type it, then click "predict".
steps.why: The percent yield: what you got over what the equation says you could get, from the reagent that runs out first, the limiting one.

steps.title: The plan
steps.text: Open the notebook's planner. Type the target Cu(OH)2 and 0.600 g: step 1 is the precipitation, CuSO4 + 2 NaOH. It needs 0.00615 mol of CuSO4 (as many moles of the blue crystals: 1.536 g of CuSO4.5H2O) and 0.0123 mol of NaOH (12.3 mL of the 1.00 M base). Close the notebook.
steps.why: Worked back from what you want: the equation's ratios turn the product's moles into each reagent's.

steps.title: The beaker on the balance
steps.text: Close the notebook. Pick up the reaction beaker and click the balance; right-click the balance and click "tare".

checks.text: the beaker on the balance, tared

steps.title: About 1.54 g of the crystals
steps.text: Pick up the jar of crystals and right-click the beaker; type 1.54 and click "tip in the solid".

steps.title: What the balance says
steps.text: Right-click the balance and click "+ mass": what you took.

steps.title: Dissolved
steps.text: Pick up the beaker and set it on the bench. Pick up the water and right-click the beaker; type 50 and click "pour". Right-click the beaker and click "stir".

steps.title: The base, in excess
steps.text: Pick up the sodium hydroxide and right-click the beaker; type 15 and click "pour": more than the 12.3 mL the plan needs, so the copper runs out first.
steps.why: Copper hydroxide hardly dissolves: it comes out as a pale blue powder at once. With the base in excess, the copper sulfate is the limiting reagent: the yield is reckoned from it.

checks.text: the copper all out of the solution

steps.title: The funnel on the flask
steps.text: Pick up the filter funnel and click the flask.

steps.title: Pour it through
steps.text: Pick up the stirred beaker and right-click the funnel; type 100 and click "pour": all of it.

steps.title: The rest of the powder
steps.text: Pick up the beaker again and right-click the funnel; click "tip in the solid".

steps.title: Until it has drained
steps.text: Wait while the filtrate drips through.

steps.title: The dish on the balance
steps.text: Pick up the weighing dish and click the balance; right-click the balance and click "tare".

checks.text: the dish on the balance, tared

steps.title: The powder into the dish
steps.text: Pick up the funnel and right-click the dish; click "tip in the solid".

steps.title: Its mass, and the yield
steps.text: Right-click the balance and click "+ mass". In the calculator's "reaction", choose CuSO4 + 2 NaOH: type the CuSO4 you used (the crystals' mass x 159.60 / 249.68) and what you got: it gives the yield.

report.label: the percent yield of copper hydroxide
report.truth: 100 * dish.copper_hydroxide.g / (97.56 * (dish.copper_hydroxide.mol + funnel.copper_hydroxide.mol + beaker.copper_hydroxide.mol + beaker.copper_sulfate_aq.mol + flask.copper_sulfate_aq.mol + flask.copper_hydroxide.mol))
report.why: What you weighed over what the copper you put in could make: 97.56 g of Cu(OH)2 for each mole of the crystals. Here nearly all of it: the precipitate hardly dissolves, every grain was carried across, and the paper kept them all. A real yield is lower: powder clings to glass and paper, a little passes the paper, and a wet cake is weighed only once dried.
